items.stem: What is heredity?
items.answer: Heredity is the transmission of characters from parents to their offspring through the DNA carried in the gametes, which is why children resemble their parents.

items.stem: Why is a trait acquired during life not inherited?
items.answer: Because it changes only the body cells and not the DNA of the germ cells. Only the DNA in the gametes passes to the next generation, so a change confined to body tissue disappears with the individual.

items.stem: What is a recessive trait?
items.answer: A recessive trait is one that is hidden when the dominant factor is present, and shows itself only when both factors present are of the recessive kind.

items.stem: What did Mendel mean by a factor, and what do we call it today?
items.answer: Mendel proposed that each character is controlled by a pair of independent units passed from the parents, which he called factors. Today these are called genes, and they are segments of DNA on the chromosomes.

items.stem: Write the genotype ratio obtained in the second generation of a monohybrid cross.
items.answer: One pure dominant to two hybrids to one pure recessive, that is 1 to 2 to 1. The visible ratio is 3 to 1 because the hybrids look like the pure dominants.

items.stem: Give two sources of variation in sexually reproducing organisms.
items.answer: Errors during the copying of DNA, which produce new differences, and the combining and reshuffling of chromosomes from two parents during gamete formation and fertilisation, which produces new combinations of existing differences.

items.stem: What does the law of independent assortment state, and what evidence supports it?
items.answer: It states that the factors for two different characters are inherited independently of each other. The evidence is Mendel's dihybrid cross, which produced round-green and wrinkled-yellow peas that had not existed in either parent, showing that shape and colour were not passed on as a fixed pair.

items.stem: Why is it scientifically wrong to blame a mother for the sex of her child?
items.answer: Every egg carries an X chromosome, so the mother can only ever contribute an X. The sperm carries either an X or a Y, and which one fertilises the egg decides the sex. The determination therefore rests entirely with the father's chromosome, and in any case the outcome is a matter of chance.

items.stem: Why was the garden pea a good choice for Mendel's experiments?
items.answer: Several features made it suitable. It has a number of clearly contrasting characters, such as tall and short plants, round and wrinkled seeds, and yellow and green seeds, with no intermediate forms to complicate the counting. It is normally self-pollinating, so pure lines that breed true could be established and maintained. At the same time it can be cross-pollinated by hand, since the flower is large enough for the anthers to be removed and pollen to be applied deliberately, so the experimenter controls which plants are crossed. It grows quickly and produces many seeds, so large numbers could be counted and the results treated statistically rather than anecdotally. Finally it is easy to grow in a garden, so many generations could be raised. Mendel's insight was as much in the choice of organism and in counting large numbers as in the interpretation.

items.stem: Explain the terms dominant and recessive with reference to a monohybrid cross.
items.answer: Take a cross between a pure tall pea plant and a pure short one. Every plant in the first generation is tall, so tallness is the dominant trait, meaning the one that shows itself when both factors are present. Shortness is the recessive trait, meaning the one that is hidden in that situation. Crucially, recessive does not mean lost. When the first-generation tall plants are crossed among themselves, the second generation contains both tall and short plants in a ratio of about three to one. The reappearance of shortness proves that the factor for it survived unchanged through the first generation while being masked. This is why Mendel concluded that a plant carries two factors for each character and that they remain independent rather than blending, since blending would have given medium-height plants and the original forms could never have returned.

items.stem: Work through a monohybrid cross between a pure tall and a pure short pea plant to the second generation.
items.answer: Let T be the factor for tallness, which is dominant, and t that for shortness. The pure tall parent is TT and the pure short parent is tt. Each parent produces gametes carrying one factor, so all gametes from the first are T and all from the second are t. Every offspring in the first generation is therefore Tt, a hybrid, and since T is dominant all of them are tall; shortness has disappeared from view. Now cross two of these first-generation plants. Each produces two kinds of gamete, T and t, in equal numbers. Combining them gives four equally likely outcomes: TT, Tt, tT and tt. So the genotypes occur in the ratio one TT to two Tt to one tt. Since TT and Tt both look tall and only tt looks short, the visible ratio is three tall to one short. The result explains two things at once: why shortness vanished in the first generation and why it returned in one quarter of the second.

items.stem: Describe Mendel's dihybrid cross and state what it established.
items.answer: Mendel crossed a pea plant having round yellow seeds with one having wrinkled green seeds, both pure breeding. The first generation was entirely round and yellow, showing that roundness and yellowness are the dominant traits. He then crossed the first-generation plants among themselves. The second generation contained four kinds of seed in a ratio of approximately nine round yellow, three round green, three wrinkled yellow and one wrinkled green. The important point is the appearance of round green and wrinkled yellow seeds, since neither combination existed in either grandparent. Had shape and colour been inherited together as a package, only the two original combinations could ever have appeared. Their separation establishes that the factors for two different characters are inherited independently of each other, which is the law of independent assortment. The nine to three to three to one ratio is itself the product of two independent three to one ratios, which is a further confirmation of independence.

items.stem: Explain the relationship between DNA, genes and chromosomes.
items.answer: DNA is the long molecule in which hereditary information is written. A gene is a particular segment of that DNA, and it carries the information for one protein, usually an enzyme, which in turn controls some characteristic of the body. Chromosomes are the structures in which the DNA is packaged inside the nucleus, each being a very long DNA molecule with associated protein. In a human body cell there are 46 chromosomes arranged as 23 pairs, one member of each pair having come from the mother and one from the father. Because the chromosomes are paired, the genes on them are paired too, which is the physical basis of Mendel's two factors for each character. When gametes are formed the pairs separate, so a gamete carries 23 single chromosomes and therefore one factor of each pair, and fertilisation restores the pairs in the zygote. This is why the number does not double at each generation, and it is what Mendel's law of segregation describes without his having known the chromosomes existed.

items.stem: Explain how variations accumulate over generations and why this matters.
items.answer: Consider a single bacterium dividing. Its two offspring are nearly identical to it, differing only by the small errors made when the DNA was copied. Those two divide in turn, and their four offspring inherit the earlier differences and add new ones of their own. Continue for many generations and the differences compound, so that the individuals in the final generation differ from one another and from the original, even though each step involved only a slight change. In sexually reproducing organisms the accumulation is far faster, because fertilisation combines the accumulated variations of two separate lineages and gamete formation reshuffles them, creating combinations that neither parent possessed. This matters because it is the mechanism by which a population becomes capable of surviving conditions it has never met. No organism can be designed in advance for a change that has not yet happened, so the only available protection is to contain individuals that differ. When conditions change, those whose accumulated variation happens to suit the new situation survive and reproduce, and the population continues in an altered form. Accumulated variation is thus the raw material of evolution, and it is worth noting that it depends on reproduction being not quite perfect: entirely faithful copying would leave a species with no capacity to change at all.

items.stem: Explain how a gene controls a characteristic, using plant height as the example.
items.answer: A gene is a segment of DNA carrying the information for making one protein, and most such proteins are enzymes that carry out a particular chemical step in the cell. Plant height depends on the amount of a growth hormone the plant can produce, and that production requires an enzyme. The gene for tallness codes for an efficient form of that enzyme, so enough hormone is made and the plant grows tall. The recessive form of the gene codes for a less efficient enzyme, so less hormone is made. Now consider the three possible pairings. A plant with two dominant factors makes plenty of the efficient enzyme and is tall. A plant with one of each still has one working copy, which produces enough hormone for full height, so it too is tall; this is exactly why the dominant trait shows in a hybrid while the recessive factor is present but hidden. A plant with two recessive factors has no efficient copy at all, makes too little hormone, and is short. The explanation matters because it shows that dominance is not a mysterious property of a trait but a consequence of how enzymes work: one functioning copy of a gene is often sufficient, and that sufficiency is what makes the other version recessive.

items.stem: Explain how sex is determined in human beings and assess the social consequences of misunderstanding it.
items.answer: Of the 23 pairs of chromosomes in a human cell, 22 pairs are alike in both sexes and the last pair differs. A female has two X chromosomes and a male has one X and one Y. When gametes form, the pair separates, so every egg produced by a mother carries an X, since that is all she has to give. A father produces two kinds of sperm in equal numbers, half carrying X and half carrying Y. If an X-bearing sperm fertilises the egg the child is XX and female; if a Y-bearing sperm does so the child is XY and male. The determination therefore rests entirely on which of the father's two kinds of sperm reaches the egg first, and since the two kinds are equally numerous the chance is close to even. The social consequences of misunderstanding this have been severe. In many places a mother is blamed for bearing daughters, which is biologically impossible since she can contribute only an X, and the belief has been used to justify neglect, cruelty and abandonment. The same prejudice has driven the misuse of prenatal diagnostic techniques to determine sex followed by the abortion of female foetuses, which has distorted the sex ratio in parts of the country to an extent that will take generations to correct, and which is why the practice is prohibited by law. A correct understanding of a simple piece of chromosome biology is therefore not merely academic; it removes the factual basis of a serious social harm.

items.answer: genes

items.stem: Explain what heredity is, how characters are transmitted, and how inherited traits differ from acquired ones.
items.answer: Heredity is the transmission of characters from parents to offspring, and it is the reason children resemble their parents. The mechanism is the DNA carried in the gametes. DNA is the molecule in which the information for building the body is written, and a gene is a segment of it that carries the information for one protein, usually an enzyme that controls some characteristic. The DNA is packaged into chromosomes, of which a human body cell has 46 arranged in 23 pairs, one member of each pair inherited from each parent. When gametes form, the pairs separate so that each gamete carries 23 single chromosomes, and fertilisation restores the pairs. The offspring therefore receives one complete set from each parent and shows characters drawn from both. An inherited trait is one written in this DNA, such as eye colour or blood group, and it passes to the next generation. An acquired trait is one gained during the individual's own life, such as a scar, a learnt skill or weight lost by dieting. It changes only the body cells and leaves the DNA of the gametes untouched, so it cannot be transmitted. This is why cutting the tails of mice for many generations never produces a tailless mouse, and it is a crucial distinction, because only inherited variation can contribute to the long-term change of a species.

items.stem: Describe Mendel's monohybrid experiment in full, giving the crosses, the results and the conclusions.
items.answer: Mendel began with pure-breeding pea plants, one line always tall and another always short, established by allowing them to self-pollinate over several generations. He then cross-pollinated a tall plant with a short one. Every plant in the resulting first generation was tall, and no plant of intermediate height appeared. This was the first surprise, since a blending theory of inheritance would have predicted medium plants. He then allowed the first-generation plants to self-pollinate. The second generation contained both tall and short plants, in a ratio of about three tall to one short across large numbers, and the short plants were exactly as short as the original short grandparents rather than being partly tall. Mendel drew three conclusions. First, each plant carries two factors for height, one received from each parent. Second, of the two, one may be dominant and show itself while the other is recessive and is hidden; tallness is dominant and shortness recessive. Third, the recessive factor is not destroyed or diluted but persists unchanged, which is why shortness disappears in the first generation and returns in a quarter of the second. Writing T for tall and t for short: the parents are TT and tt, all first-generation plants are Tt and therefore tall, and crossing Tt with Tt gives TT, Tt, tT and tt in equal numbers, that is genotypes in the ratio 1 to 2 to 1 and appearances in the ratio 3 tall to 1 short. The reasoning depended on counting large numbers, since the ratio emerges statistically and would not be visible in a handful of plants.

items.stem: Explain the physical basis of Mendel's two laws in terms of chromosomes, and note what Mendel could not have known.
items.answer: Mendel proposed that each character is controlled by a pair of factors which separate during gamete formation, and that the pairs for different characters separate independently of one another. He had no way of seeing either process; the chromosomes had not yet been described. The physical basis was established later. Chromosomes occur in pairs in a body cell, one member of each pair from each parent, and a gene is a segment of DNA at a particular place on a chromosome. Since the chromosomes are paired, the genes on them are paired too, and this is Mendel's two factors for each character. During the formation of gametes the members of each pair separate and go to different gametes, so a gamete receives one chromosome of each pair and therefore one factor of each gene. This is the law of segregation, and it explains why the gamete carries 23 chromosomes when the body cell has 46, and why fertilisation restores the number rather than doubling it. The second law follows from the fact that different pairs of chromosomes separate independently: which member of one pair a gamete receives has no bearing on which member of another pair it receives, so the factors for two characters on different chromosome pairs are inherited independently. This is the law of independent assortment, and the dihybrid ratio of nine to three to three to one is the arithmetic consequence of two independent three-to-one ratios. Two things Mendel could not have known are worth stating. He could not know that his laws hold only for genes on different chromosome pairs, since genes lying close together on the same chromosome tend to be inherited together and do not assort independently. And he could not know the mechanism of dominance, which turns out to be that one working copy of a gene often produces enough enzyme for the full effect, making the other version recessive. That his conclusions survived the discovery of the mechanism is a measure of how carefully they were drawn from counting alone.

items.stem: Assess the role of variation and inheritance in allowing a species to survive a changing environment.
items.answer: Two things are required for a species to persist through change, and they pull in different directions. The first is fidelity. The design of a successful organism must be reproduced accurately, or each generation would be a fresh experiment and the advantages already achieved would be lost. Inheritance through DNA provides this, since copying is remarkably accurate and the offspring closely resemble the parents. The second is variability. Conditions do change, through climate, disease, predators or the loss of a food source, and no organism can be designed in advance for a change that has not yet occurred. If every individual were identical, then whatever lay outside the tolerance of one would lie outside the tolerance of all, and a single change could end the species. Variation provides the insurance, since a population whose individuals differ is likely to contain some that cope. The sources of variation are the small errors in DNA copying, which introduce genuinely new differences, and in sexually reproducing organisms the combining of DNA from two parents and the reshuffling of chromosomes during gamete formation, which creates new combinations of existing differences on a far larger scale. These accumulate across generations, because each generation inherits what went before and adds its own. The assessment, then, is that neither fidelity nor variability alone would serve. Perfect copying would preserve a design until the first serious change destroyed it. Very high variation would destroy the design immediately, since most changes are harmful. What is observed is an intermediate rate, high enough to supply differences and low enough to keep the design intact, and the survival of a species depends on that balance rather than on either property by itself. It also follows that the environment does not create the variation it selects: the differences arise independently, and the change merely determines which of them happens to be useful.

items.stem: In the second generation of a monohybrid cross, 1600 plants are obtained. How many are expected to be short?
items.answer: The expected ratio is three tall to one short, so short plants are one quarter of the total. One quarter of 1600 is 400 short plants, with 1200 expected to be tall.

items.stem: A dihybrid cross gives 640 seeds in the second generation. Find the expected number of each of the four kinds.
items.answer: The expected ratio is nine to three to three to one, making sixteen parts in all. One part is 640 divided by 16, which is 40. So round yellow is 9 times 40, which is 360; round green is 3 times 40, which is 120; wrinkled yellow is also 120; and wrinkled green is 1 times 40, which is 40. Checking, 360 plus 120 plus 120 plus 40 gives 640, as required.

items.stem: A couple has three daughters. Find the probability that a fourth child will be a daughter, and explain your reasoning.
items.answer: The probability is one half. Each fertilisation is an independent event: the mother contributes an X in every case, and the father produces X-bearing and Y-bearing sperm in equal numbers, so the chance of either outcome is one half every time. The three previous daughters do not alter the composition of the father's sperm and the sperm carry no record of earlier births, so the fourth conception starts afresh. Believing otherwise is the gambler's fallacy. It is worth adding that the probability of four daughters in a row is one half raised to the power four, which is one sixteenth, and this is a perfectly ordinary outcome that requires no special explanation; roughly one family in sixteen with four children will have four daughters.

items.answer: (a) plant height - (iii) tall. (b) seed shape - (i) round. (c) seed colour - (iv) yellow. (d) pod shape - (ii) inflated.

items.stem: Draw a labelled cross diagram for a monohybrid cross to the second generation, showing all genotypes.
items.answer: Draw three labelled rows. In the parent row, write the two pure parents as TT for tall and tt for short, labelling T as the dominant factor for tallness and t as the recessive factor for shortness. Below each, show the gametes in circles: all T from the first and all t from the second, and label the row gametes. Draw arrows converging to the first generation and write Tt, noting beside it that all plants are tall because T is dominant and that shortness is hidden but not lost. Now draw a second gamete row from two first-generation plants, showing T and t from each. Below this draw a two-by-two grid, writing T and t across the top for one parent's gametes and T and t down the side for the other's. Fill the four boxes with TT, Tt, tT and tt. Annotate the grid: label TT pure tall, the two Tt boxes hybrid tall, and tt pure short. Below the grid write the genotype ratio 1 to 2 to 1 and the phenotype ratio 3 tall to 1 short, with a note that the ratios differ because the hybrids look identical to the pure dominants. Add a final annotation that the reappearance of tt proves the recessive factor survived the first generation unchanged.

items.stem: Draw a labelled diagram of sex determination in humans and annotate it to show where the outcome is decided.
items.answer: Draw two parent boxes at the top. Label the left one mother, with the sex chromosomes XX, and the right one father, with XY. Below the mother, draw one kind of gamete in a circle containing X, and annotate that every egg carries an X because that is all she has to give. Below the father, draw two kinds of gamete in circles, one containing X and one containing Y, and annotate that the two kinds are produced in equal numbers. Now draw arrows from the mother's single gamete to each of the father's two gametes, and below each pairing write the resulting zygote: XX from the first and XY from the second. Label XX as female and XY as male, and write one half beneath each to show that the two outcomes are equally likely. Add a clear annotation with an arrow pointing to the father's gamete row reading: the outcome is decided here, by which of the two kinds of sperm reaches the egg. Add a second annotation with an arrow to the mother's gamete reading: the mother cannot influence the outcome, since she contributes only X. Finish with a note that each fertilisation is independent of any earlier one, so previous children do not change the probability, and a note that determining sex before birth for the purpose of selective abortion is prohibited by law.

items.stem: Show from Mendel's results that the factor for a recessive trait is not lost in the first generation.
items.answer: Take the monohybrid cross between a pure tall pea plant and a pure short one. In the first generation every plant is tall and not one is short, so on the face of it shortness has disappeared. Suppose, for the sake of argument, that the factor for shortness were destroyed or diluted away when the two parents were crossed. Two consequences would follow. First, the first-generation plants would carry nothing but factors for tallness, so crossing them among themselves could produce only tall plants, and shortness could never reappear in any later generation. Second, if instead the two factors had blended, the first generation would have been of intermediate height and the second generation would have shown a spread of heights, with the original extremes absent. Now compare these predictions with what Mendel actually observed. The second generation contained short plants, in a proportion of about one in four across large numbers. Moreover those short plants were exactly as short as the original short grandparents, not partly tall, and when self-pollinated they bred true, producing only short offspring. Neither prediction survives. Shortness reappeared, so the factor was not destroyed. The plants were of the two original heights and not intermediate, so the factors had not blended. The only account consistent with the observations is that each first-generation plant carried both factors, one for tallness and one for shortness, that the factor for tallness showed itself while the other was masked, and that the two remained separate and unchanged. When gametes were formed the pair separated so that each gamete carried one factor, and a quarter of the second-generation plants received a factor for shortness from both parents and were therefore short. This is the law of segregation, and the reappearance of an unchanged recessive trait after a generation of complete absence is its proof.
